content: The text provided is a detailed and technical description of various studies, systematic reviews, and methodologies related to the use of pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) for HIV prevention among different populations, including people who inject drugs (PWID), men who have sex with men (MSM), and other high-risk groups. 1. The use of pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) among drug users from high-risk populations for HIV in Western China was explored in a study published in the Academic Journal of Second Military Medical University in 2012. The study highlights the potential role of PrEP in reducing HIV transmission in this demographic. 2. Zhou et al. (2012) investigated the willingness of Chinese men who have sex with men (MSM) to accept HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis. Their findings, published in PLoS One, emphasize the importance of understanding attitudes toward PrEP in this population to enhance its uptake. 3. Sineath et al. (2013) examined the knowledge and interest in using PrEP for HIV prevention among MSM in Thailand. Published in the Journal of the International Association of Providers of AIDS Care, the study underscores the need for targeted education and awareness campaigns to increase PrEP utilization. 4. Tangmunkongvorakul et al. (2013) identified facilitators and barriers to medication adherence in an HIV prevention study among MSM in Chiang Mai, Thailand. Their research, part of the iPrEx study, was published in AIDS Care and provides insights into improving adherence strategies for PrEP. 5. Wheelock et al. (2013) analyzed the willingness of Thai MSM to take PrEP for HIV prevention. Their study, published in PLoS One, explored attitudes, preferences, and acceptance, offering valuable data for tailoring PrEP programs to this population. 6. Yang et al. (2013) assessed the acceptability of PrEP among MSM and transgender women in Northern Thailand. Published in PLoS One, the study highlights the potential for PrEP to address HIV prevention needs in these groups. 7. Galea et al. (2011) explored the acceptability of PrEP as an HIV prevention strategy among at-risk populations in Peru. Their findings, published in the International Journal of STD & AIDS, identified barriers and facilitators to PrEP uptake. 8. Peinado et al. (2013) compared the acceptability of oral versus rectal PrEP among MSM and transgender women in Peru. Published in the Journal of the International Association of Providers of AIDS Care, the study provides critical insights into preferences for PrEP delivery methods. 9. Liu and Sanchez (2012) presented findings on the willingness to use PrEP among high-risk MSM in Lima, Peru, at the 19th International AIDS Conference in Washington, DC. Their research highlights the need for targeted interventions in this population. 10. Lorente et al. (2012) investigated the acceptability of an on-demand PrEP trial among MSM in France. Published in AIDS Care, the study provides evidence for alternative PrEP dosing strategies. 11. Rosenthal et al. (2013) conducted a nationwide cross-sectional study in France (PREVIC study) to evaluate the use of PrEP for HIV prevention. Their findings, published in AIDS Care, offer insights into the implementation of PrEP at a national level. 12. Aghaizu et al. (2013) examined factors associated with the intention to use PrEP among MSM in London through a community survey. Published in Sexually Transmitted Infections, the study highlights predictors of PrEP uptake. 13. Thng et al. (2012) assessed the acceptability of PrEP and associated risk compensation behaviors among MSM accessing genitourinary services. Published in HIV Medicine, the study provides insights into the potential impact of PrEP on sexual health behaviors. 14. Holt et al. (2013) explored attitudes toward HIV treatments and antiretroviral-based prevention among HIV-negative and HIV-positive gay men in Australia. Published in AIDS Behavior, the study highlights the role of perceptions in shaping PrEP uptake. 15. Holt et al. (2012) also examined the willingness to use PrEP and its association with decreased condom use among Australian gay and bisexual men. Published in Sexually Transmitted Infections, the study underscores the need for comprehensive sexual health education alongside PrEP. 16. Van der Elst et al. (2013) reported high acceptability of PrEP but challenges in adherence among at-risk populations in Kenya. Published in AIDS Behavior, the study provides qualitative insights into barriers to PrEP use. 17. A survey conducted by P. Ndegwa (2013) in Kenya explored community opinions and preferences regarding PrEP, microbicides, and vaccines. Presented at the 7th IAS Conference on HIV Pathogenesis, Treatment, and Prevention, the findings emphasize the importance of community engagement in HIV prevention strategies. 18. Leonardi et al. (2011) assessed awareness, usage, and willingness to use PrEP among men in downtown Toronto, Canada. Published in the International Journal of STD & AIDS, the study highlights gaps in knowledge and the potential for PrEP uptake. 19. Krznaric and Knecht (2013) investigated attitudes toward PrEP among MSM in Germany. Presented at the 7th IAS Conference, the study provides insights into cultural and regional differences in PrEP acceptance. 20. Krakower et al. (2012) explored anticipated risk compensation behaviors with PrEP use among North American MSM using an internet social network. Published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society, the study highlights concerns about behavioral changes associated with PrEP. 21. Mimiaga and Mayer (2013) reported limited awareness but high interest in PrEP among MSM in Latin America, Spain, and Portugal using an internet social networking site. Presented at the 7th IAS Conference, the findings underscore the need for targeted education campaigns. 22. Eisingerich et al. (2012) conducted a multinational study on attitudes and acceptance of oral and parenteral PrEP among potential user groups. Published in PLoS One, the study provides a global perspective on PrEP implementation. 23. Arreola and Ayala (2012) examined social and structural barriers to PrEP, HIV testing, and treatment access among gay and other MSM in the Global South and North. Presented at the 19th International AIDS Conference, the study highlights disparities in access to HIV prevention tools. 24. Tellalian et al. (2013) surveyed HIV healthcare providers to evaluate their knowledge, attitudes, and prescribing practices for PrEP. Published in AIDS Patient Care and STDs, the study identifies gaps in provider readiness for PrEP implementation. 25. Karris et al. (2013) assessed provider opinions on the real-world use of PrEP in the United States and Canada. Published in Clinical Infectious Diseases, the study highlights challenges in scaling up PrEP. 26. Kapur et al. (2012) evaluated the knowledge, attitudes, and willingness of New York City providers to prescribe oral PrEP for HIV prevention. Presented at the 19th International AIDS Conference, the study underscores the importance of provider education. 27. Arnold et al. (2012) conducted a qualitative study on provider perspectives on implementing PrEP in clinical settings. Published in PLoS One, the study provides insights into the practical challenges of PrEP delivery. 28. Calabrese et al. (2013) examined the impact of patient race on clinical decisions related to prescribing PrEP. Published in AIDS Behavior, the study highlights the role of implicit biases in healthcare access. 29. Tang et al. (2013) explored provider attitudes toward oral PrEP for high-risk MSM in Lima, Peru. Published in AIDS Research and Human Retroviruses, the study provides insights into regional differences in PrEP implementation. 30. Taegtmeyer et al. (2013) reported challenges in providing counseling to MSM in highly stigmatized contexts in Kenya. Published in PLoS One, the study underscores the need for stigma reduction to improve PrEP access.
